1:
The speaker has stopped counting in years. Henry notices the correction: a few chapters earlier it was when a few years have come I shall go that long journey, and here the journey has already begun, the man now ready to be offered. The breath of life is continually going forth, standing in the nostrils at the very door by which it entered, and a distemper that obstructs the breathing turns short breath into no breath at all; the days are put out like a candle that wastes from the moment it is lit and may be quenched by a thousand accidents. Gill works the same clause medically, taking the corruption for an ill smell that made the man strange to his wife, noting that the Hebrew word carries pain, even the pains of a woman in travail, so that it may mean breath drawn with difficulty as in asthma; and he allows the alternatives, my spirit, meaning vital spirits spent, or my mind, overwhelmed with grief and in a manner distracted by the terrors of God. Ellicott says only that this is what happens in elephantiasis, and reports the reading my spirit is consumed. Clarke prefers my spirit is oppressed, and collects manuscripts reading made weak or worn down, with the Latin version giving exhausted.

The graves come next, and the plural is the problem. Henry asks whether one grave would not serve, and answers that these are the sepulchres of the fathers, graves in consort, the congregation of the dead to which this man must be gathered; wherever we go there is but a step between us and them, and whatever else is unready the grave is ready, being a bed soon made, so that if the graves are ready for us it concerns us to be ready for the graves. He hears in the phrase not only an expectation of death but a desire for it, a man done with the world who has nothing left to wish for but a grave. Wesley repeats the point about the fathers' sepulchres and the bed soon made almost word for word. Ellicott treats the plural as Hebrew idiom, standing for a singular as the word for blood commonly does, so that the sense is simply the grave is mine, my portion. Clarke reads the same noun as sepulchral cells, with a probable reference to cemeteries where several niches each held a corpse.

The complaint about mockers is where the voices divide, and the division is textual rather than doctrinal. Gill rules out the obvious targets, the men who make a mock at sin and scoff at things to come, and fixes on the friends, by whom this man thought himself mocked, which is why he asks for his case to be heard. Wesley puts it as the question it is, whether his friends, instead of comforting, mock him. Ellicott renders the second clause as a bitter reproach: the eye sees nothing else and has nothing else to look upon. Clarke, by contrast, finds the line so uncertain that he simply lists what has been made of it, the Latin version's I have not sinned and yet my eye dwells upon afflictions, the Greek's I conjure you, what evil have I done, Calmet's conjecture about friendship with the wicked, Coverdale's I have deceived no man yet must mine eye continue in heaviness, and two renderings of his own day, before concluding drily that the general meaning is plain and the reader has translations enough. Delitzsch defends the chapter division against those who would move it, since the previous verse closes a strain and a new one begins here; and he refuses Ewald's my spirit is destroyed, because the verb means not destroyed but corrupted or troubled, and the subject is the breath, grown short and offensive, announcing suffocation and decay as no longer far off.
3:
The request is for a pledge, and Ellicott gives it the fullest reading in the chapter. Having claimed a witness in the heavens, the man now wants some present token of the vindication he is sure of, and so asks God to be surety for him with himself, which Ellicott matches to Hezekiah's prayer, undertake for me. There is that in man, he says, which demands exact fulfilment or expiation of non-fulfilment, and this man felt that his only hope of either lay with the very God who had put that sense of obligation in him; having earlier longed for a daysman to lay a hand on both parties, he now longs for a surety that God alone can give, since a witness in the heavens requires a divine surety, the witness of God to God himself. Ellicott remarks how strangely the language fits what has since been learnt of the persons in the Godhead, and notes that striking hands was the form the transaction took, which is why the question is asked at all: nobody among the friends would do it, or could if he would. Gill reads the opening word as a request that God put his heart and mind to the case and admit someone to plead it. Wesley takes it as a humble desire that God either be the surety or appoint one. Clarke turns the words outward instead, as a challenge to the friends to stake their conduct and their souls against his and see which of them is justified when the cause comes before God.

Why the friends cannot serve as judges is answered in one line, and the voices divide over who did the hiding. Gill takes the hearts to be the friends' and the hiding to be God's, and sets it among God's other acts of the kind: he gives men up to minds void of natural judgment when they will not know him, he hides divine things from the wise and prudent of this world, and he sometimes hides even the meaning of his own providences from his own people, as from Asaph and Jeremiah and Habakkuk, and here from men who therefore mistook the case entirely. Clarke will not have the verb pressed so far, since God is here represented as doing what in the course of his providence he only permits; and he points out that the clause about not exalting them was fulfilled exactly, no one of these friends being exalted but all of them condemned, and not received into favour until the man they accused sacrificed and interceded for them. Wesley keeps the plain sense and draws the inference the speaker wants, that a judge more wise and able is needed, and that the friends will not be given the victory but made ashamed of their confidence.

The verse about flattery defeats everyone, and two of them say so. Ellicott calls the three Hebrew words most obscure from their very brevity, renders them literally as for a portion he will tell friends, and reports two attempts at sense: that the friends are denounced for a prey, or that any surety would expect the friends to share the liability, whereas in fact the sons' eyes would fail in looking for it and they would never see it. Clarke notes the same variety of opinion and settles for a general moral, that a man who expects much from his friends will be disappointed, and may leave his children looking for bread while he waits. Gill alone treats the clause as a charge with specific content, identifying two flatteries in what the friends had said: the promise of outward prosperity and restoration on condition of repentance, and the deceitful speaking for God that pretended a regard for his justice while insisting that an afflicted man must be wicked and a hypocrite.
6:
Becoming a byword is the first grievance, and Gill observes that it came true in a way the speaker could not have meant. Whether the agent was Eliphaz or God, he ascribes it to God as suffered in providence; and the name has remained a proverb for poverty and for patience alike, neither of which is a disgrace, so that something more reproachful must be intended here. Clarke reports the proverbs as still current in his own day, then refuses the received rendering of the second clause: it is not what the Hebrew says, and by reading one pronoun differently he would have the man become a furnace or consuming fire before his friends, who will have little reason to mock when they see the end of the Lord's dealings. He adds Coverdale's blunter version, that he is their jesting stock. Ellicott keeps the drum and makes it a signal of warning, a case fraught with warning for others, while reporting the rival reading that it means an open abhorrence, one in whose face they spit; the general sense, he says, is clear however it is put. Delitzsch settles the word etymologically, dismissing the older expositors who heard in it the place of the Moloch sacrifices in the valley of the sons of Hinnom and so glossed it the fire of hell, and deriving it from a verb meaning to spit out, scarcely attested in Hebrew outside two passages in the Talmud but confirmed by Ethiopic and Coptic, by the onomatopoeia of the Greek and Latin words for spitting, and by an Arabic verb meaning to treat with contempt.

The body is described next, and briefly. Gill has the eye dimmed by excessive weeping until the sight was nearly gone; Clarke generalises, since continual weeping impairs the sight and any affliction that weakens the frame weakens the eyes in proportion, and reads the shadow as literally as it can be taken, nothing left but skin and bone, a man become the shadow of his former self. What that spectacle does to onlookers is where the chapter turns outward. Gill expects the astonishment of men upright in heart, amazed both at the afflictions and at the unkindness of the friends, and thinks the surprise will persist into later ages, when people will hardly know how to believe such afflictions laid on so good a man, still less account for their being permitted. Wesley locates the astonishment precisely, in the depth and mysteriousness of judgments that fall on innocent men while the worst of men prosper, and has the innocent respond by opposing the more zealously those hypocrites who make such providences an objection to religion.

The last verse of the stanza is read as a prophecy, and Clarke makes the most of it. He takes several of these verses as spoken in foresight of the restoration to come and of the good religious society would draw from the whole history, affluence and poverty and recovery together: the upright will receive the account with astonishment while false professors are unmasked, and once the case is known nobody will be stumbled at seeing a godly man under oppression, since whatever happens to a righteous man he may take it for granted that all is justly managed and the end will be glorious. The righteous will draw strength from this example by every blast of adversity, and Clarke names that as one grand use of the book, which has always been the text-book of godly men under persecution. Gill describes the holding on as perseverance in a way already entered, set against going back, turning to either hand, and standing still through being stumbled or discouraged by affliction or reproach or the snares of the world. Ellicott compresses the whole sequence into its logic: the warning the case gives astonishes the upright, encourages the innocent, and makes the righteous persevere and wax bold.
10:
The friends are told to come back, and nobody agrees on the tone. Gill offers three readings: a challenge to go on with the dispute, since a man conscious of his innocence was a match for all three; a call to repent of their hard speeches and return to amicable conversation; or an invitation to sit quietly and hear what he has still to say. Clarke takes it as a dismissal, telling men too full of self-importance to profit by what they see to consider their ways and go back to school until they acquire humility and knowledge. Ellicott hears irony and sharpens the grammar to match: not I cannot find a wise man among you but I shall not find one, if you renew the argument. Wesley reads it as consent to a debate the friends are plainly resolved on. Henry goes behind the summons and makes the friends' comfort itself the folly: those do not go wisely about comforting the afflicted who fetch their comfort from the possibility of recovery in this world, which is uncertain at best, so that if it fails the comfort fails with it. The wisdom, he says, is to comfort ourselves with what will not fail, the promise of God and a well-grounded hope of eternal life.

The comfort is useless because the man reckons himself already finished. Henry lists what he had meant to do, enlarging his border, increasing his stock, settling his children, promoting religion in his country, redressing grievances, relieving the poor, all broken off with the days that were to have held them; the period of our days, he observes, is the period of all our contrivances for this world, though if we cleave to the Lord with full purpose of heart, death does not break off that purpose. Gill is careful that no day was actually passed, since the bound God sets cannot be overstepped, and reads the clause either of the common term of human life or of the man's own apprehension; he then turns it into evidence for the charge just made, since friends who promise long life on repentance are the ones with no wisdom in them. Clarke calls this a relapse into the former gloom and notes how frequent such transitions are in the poem, marking the struggle of piety against continued affliction and gloomy providences. Wesley states the conclusion the speaker draws: a dying man has no use for their hopes.

The last verse divides them over who changes night into day. Gill allows either the friends or the man's own thoughts, which he says comes to one thing, since thoughts busy all night with what was said in the day leave the night as broad as day; and he reports a reading by which the friends put day before night, against the order of nature, promising an age clearer than noon. Henry keeps the thoughts and makes the exchange a double loss, the repose of the night gone so that its tossings tire a man as much as the day's toils, and the day's entertainment gone too, since inward darkness spoils the morning light; which is reason enough, he adds, to be thankful for health that lets us welcome evening and morning equally. Wesley says the same briefly: thoughts that will not stop make night and day alike. Clarke hears the second clause differently, rendering it that the light is near from the face of darkness, so that what light there is lies too close to darkness to be severed from it, which he calls a fine picture of a mind generally dark with occasional gleams of hope. Ellicott gives the clause to the friends: so little did they enter into the case that they wanted the man to believe his night of trial was the reverse of darkness and light at hand, which only sharpened the mockery against what he felt.
13:
Waiting is the friends' word, and Gill will not let it be read as doubt about waiting on God, which this man had determined to do. The conditional is aimed at their advice: they had held out a peaceable tabernacle and a prosperous habitation on terms of repentance, and Gill asks how long such a hope would last, when no other house can be expected than the one named here. Clarke puts it as a reckoning indifferent to length of days: long life or short, the grave will be home at last, and he expects soon to lie down in darkness. Wesley turns the expectation into a discipline, preparing the bed by keeping his conscience pure, by seeing Christ lying in it and so making it a bed of spices, and by looking past it to the resurrection.

The next verse makes a family of the grave's occupants. Gill rules out two other corruptions, the seed a man is begotten of and the matter of the boils, and fixes on what the body turns to in the grave, which Christ's body did not see; then he reads the figure through the household it borrows: as a house holds a family of different relations, so the grave is the dwelling house of men whose inhabitants keep company, and it is to these, corruption and rottenness and dust and worms, that a man claims kindred and speaks not only familiarly but respectfully. Clarke makes the kinship literal both ways, coming from a corrupted stock and going back to corruption, and offers his own rendering, to the ditch I have called, thou art my father, and to the worm, thou art my mother and my sister, since nothing stands nearer him now than dissolution. Wesley hears a child's claim on a parent's house: the pit will keep him as parents keep their children.

The question about hope depends on which hope is meant. Gill distinguishes sharply: not the grace of hope, an anchor sure and steadfast that never makes a man ashamed, nor the object laid up in heaven, but the hope of restored prosperity the friends had been pressing, which had no place in him and no foundation left. Clarke asks what use hope can be in such circumstances, since nobody would live to see the expectation realised. Wesley identifies it in six words as the happiness they would have him expect.

The closing verse defeats the grammarians, and Ellicott calls it the most difficult in a chapter that is itself among the most difficult. The problem is agreement: the bars of the grave are masculine while the verb is feminine plural, so they are unlikely to be its subject; yet if the bars are the destination, nothing else will serve, hope being feminine singular. Some render it shall go down, defying the grammar though probably conveying something near the truth; the rule that a verb before its subject need not agree is no help, since here the verb must follow; and the corruption and the worm just named cannot be meant, being already in the grave rather than going down to it. Clarke takes the noun differently, since the word for bars also means branches or claws, so that it may personify the grave as a monster holding bodies in its deadly gripe, or name the branching alleys of subterranean catacombs with their niches. He then explains the gloom historically: deep shades hung in those times over the state of man after death, leaving uncertainty even on the best of the older believers, the true light not yet come. Gill sends the man, his friends and their proffered hopes down together to be barred up, the hopes never to rise. Wesley finds the one consolation in it, that good men who cannot agree now will rest together there, and asks that the foresight cool the heat of all contenders.
